attribution.note: Marcus endorses the allegation of redefinition; Suleyman’s quoted words are the subject of that allegation.

semantics.note: The proposition preserves Marcus’s allegation, timing, comparison, and enterprise scope.

contract.note: Public reframing is an ordinary reading of attempted redefinition. Requiring a formal technical change would exceed Marcus’s words.

evidence.note: The dated interview directly attributes an enterprise-value criterion to Suleyman without retaining a superhuman-performance requirement in that framing.
This earlier first-person account envisages superhuman capabilities. It limits conclusions about abandonment of that conception but does not negate the April reframing.

reviews.rationale: The April interview meets the contract’s public-framing criterion. Suleyman presents enterprise product value as central to superintelligence without stating a superhuman threshold. His earlier account provides relevant context but does not contradict this narrower finding.

attribution.note: Marcus asserts the loss figure himself. The surrounding speculation concerns acquisition motives.

semantics.note: The proposition preserves the approximate ongoing monthly loss claim. Its present tense supports assessment through the post rather than as a full-year forecast.

contract.note: Net loss is a fair ordinary reading of financial losses, and the latest completed quarter reasonably tests the ongoing rate. Cash burn would produce a different assessment.

evidence.note: Reported Q1 net losses exceed $7.1 billion monthly on average, materially above the claimed rate under the contract’s ordinary net-loss reading. This is secondary reporting of shareholder documents.
Reported cash burn averages $1.23 billion monthly, close to the claimed figure but a different metric. Reuters expressly could not verify the underlying report.
The full-year projection could explain the approximation but cannot establish realized Q1 losses.

reviews.rationale: Under the contract’s fair plain reading of losses as net losses, reported Q1 losses exceed $7.1 billion monthly, far beyond reasonable approximation to $1 billion. Cash burn is near the stated rate but measures something different. The finding rests on secondary reporting of shareholder documents, not inspected financial statements.
